extracted.intended_audience: agency attorneys, legal scholars, and policymakers drafting or evaluating federal agency social media comment policies
extracted.subtask_short: agency social media comment policy review
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and drafting federal agency social-media comment policies for compliance with First Amendment doctrine and related state/federal offenses. Focuses on what speech may be removed, constitutional constraints, and practical application guidance for agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removing off‑topic comments / keeping discussion focused
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the lack of time or space limitations on agency social media sites, removing off-topic comments may be unnecessary; however, even if removing comments absorbs the time of agency staff, doing so may not be unreasonable should an agency want the discussion to remain focused and relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may remove or moderate comments to maintain relevance of discussion for the forum’s purpose; consider whether the restriction is genuinely related to the forum’s purpose and whether less restrictive measures suffice. Examine whether removal is plausibly viewpoint-neutral and justified by maintaining the site's topical focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civility codes must be narrow, objective, and definite
rubrics_metrics.description: Vague standards such as 'otherwise objectionable' or 'vulgar' chill speech and act as a prior restraint; the Supreme Court requires 'narrow, objective, and definite standards' to guide enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague terms ('offensive', 'objectionable') in policy text. Draft civility rules with specific, measurable prohibitions. Even facially narrow rules can fail if applied improperly; agencies must use extraordinary care in enforcement to avoid viewpoint discrimination or overbroad suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civility policies must satisfy intermediate scrutiny (reasonable & viewpoint neutral)
rubrics_metrics.description: A civility policy has to satisfy intermediate scrutiny, meaning it should be reasonable in light of the purpose of the forum as well as viewpoint neutral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the policy advances a significant government interest related to the forum and is applied without regard to viewpoint. Provide clear, content‑neutral justification tied to the forum's purpose and document neutral application procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Captive audience doctrine typically not applicable to social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Civility requirements in the context of advertisements in public fora have been found constitutional under the captive audience doctrine, but that doctrine does not appear to apply to social media: readers 'may escape exposure' by averting their eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on captive audience justifications for removing offensive content on social media. Consider the private/home context of readers, but remember ability to avoid exposure (e.g., scrolling away) undercuts captive‑audience treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time, place, and manner restrictions: narrow tailoring and alternative channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Time, place, and manner restrictions must be narrowly tailored to serve the government’s legitimate, content‑neutral interest, need not be the least intrusive means, and must leave open ample alternative channels of communication; context is determinative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When invoking time/place/manner, identify the specific governmental interest and show narrow tailoring. Because expression is the normal activity of agency social sites, restrictions should target only expression that interferes with normal activity (e.g., spam) and leave other channels available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spam and repetitive interruptions may be regulated as disruptive speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Spamming is the equivalent of mobbing a public meeting or continued jeers that make discussion impossible; a federal agency can regulate spam or similar interruptions or repeated statements that render blogs or sites unusable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies may target repeated postings, automated spam, and conduct that effectively silences discourse by making the site unusable. Ensure such rules are content‑neutral and narrowly tailored to preserve discussion functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscenity (Miller test) is unprotected
rubrics_metrics.description: To be properly characterized as obscene speech must pass the three‑part Miller test: (a) appeals to prurient interest under contemporary community standards; (b) depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way as defined by state law; (c) lacks serious artistic, political, or scientific value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Miller factors when assessing allegedly obscene content. Note that 'contemporary community standards' raise special questions online, but obscenity remains a category agencies may remove. Child pornography is unprotected without Miller analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indecent speech protection depends on public‑concern/ontopic status
rubrics_metrics.description: Indecent speech, if made in a public forum on an issue of public concern, is protected and should remain posted; indecent speech that does not reference an issue of public concern or the forum’s stated subject matter may be moved or removed as off‑topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate indecent speech that engages public issues (protected) from indecent but off‑topic speech (removable in a limited public forum to preserve forum purposes or protect minors). Tailor actions to forum scope and stated topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fighting words / immediate breach of the peace (Chaplinsky) and Brandenburg test for incitement
rubrics_metrics.description: Fighting words—words 'which by their very utterance inflict injury or tend to incite an immediate breach of the peace'—may be removed where they lack ideological content; Brandenburg governs incitement (advocacy directed to incite imminent lawless action and is likely to produce such action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible removal exists where language is personal epithets/abuse with no public or ideological component or where speech constitutes true threats or imminent incitement under Brandenburg. Assess speaker intent, audience, specificity, and likelihood of imminent lawless action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive, extremist, and profane speech generally protected; restrictions suspect
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no constitutional category for 'offensive' or 'controversial' speech; restrictions on speech because it is 'upsetting' are content discrimination and are inherently suspect and subject to strict scrutiny. Profanity is presumptively protected following Cohen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid categorical bans on 'offensive', 'vulgar', or 'disrespectful' speech absent a narrowly drawn compelling interest; even apparently content‑neutral bans on particular words can be applied discriminatorily and invite strict scrutiny. Enforcement consistency and context analysis are critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hate speech protected unless it crosses into unprotected incitement/ hate crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Hate speech without incitement to violence is protected speech and cannot be removed simply because it is hateful; hate crimes (criminal acts motivated by bias) and threats that meet Brandenburg can be prosecuted and removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between offensive discriminatory language (protected) and speech that constitutes true threats, imminent incitement, or criminal conduct (removable). Be mindful that leaving hate speech posted can create perceptions of endorsement; weigh legal protection against policy/mission concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyberstalking and cyberharassment may be criminal and removable
rubrics_metrics.description: Cyberstalking involves online communication exhibiting a pattern of threatening behavior; cyberharassment involves harassing messages used to torment an individual. Such conduct often meets criminal statutes in many states and should be removed, especially upon victim request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify patterns, targeted individuals, and threats. Remove or refer to law enforcement when comments approach or constitute criminal stalking/harassment. Document incidents and victim requests when taking action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation, libel, and slander standard and agency response
rubrics_metrics.description: Defamation requires a false and defamatory statement communicated to a third party, a publisher acting negligently, and damages; libel is permanent defamation and slander is oral; public figures must prove actual malice (knowing falsity or reckless disregard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should analyze context before removing allegedly defamatory comments. Consider the difficulty of proving falsity, opinion protections, public‑figure malice standard, and potential Section 230 protections. Preemptive removal risks chilling protected speech; decisions should be case‑by‑case with documented rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal attacks: removable if non‑ideological and meet unprotected categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment policies prohibiting 'personal attacks' are constitutionally sound when the attack has no ideological component (i.e., is not addressing a public issue) and falls within unprotected categories (fighting words, threats, defamation, harassment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate personal attacks that merely express opposition to public officials/issues (likely protected) from purely personal, non‑ideological attacks that inflict injury or constitute harassment. Apply neutrally and document contextual analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application and enforcement cautions — narrow policies can fail if applied improperly
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the most narrowly tailored and objective policy will fail if applied improperly. A policy forbidding profanity would not necessarily include offensive speech and may suppress views conveyed only through strong language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train moderators/legal staff on context‑sensitive analysis, maintain consistent written enforcement procedures, keep logs/justifications for removals, and avoid ad hoc or discretionary enforcement that creates viewpoint discrimination. Err on the side of leaving public‑concern speech posted unless it clearly meets an unprotected category.
